---
title: "Why ME/CFS might be norepinephrine-low but dopamine-normal"
description: "A 2026 CSF study found the catecholamine deficit in ME/CFS is selective: norepinephrine down, dopamine normal. The selectivity is the clue."
author: "Yannick Loth"
date: "2026-09-16"
categories: [Arousal system, Noradrenergic, Mechanisms]
---

Catecholamines are a family of related brain chemicals: dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. If the body simply ran low on the raw material or a shared cofactor, you would expect the whole family to fall together.

That is not what a 2026 analysis found.

Using cerebrospinal fluid from people with ME/CFS and related conditions, Aregawi and colleagues built composite indices for the two main pathways. The **norepinephrine pathway** (norepinephrine plus its metabolites DHPG and MHPG) was significantly lower in post-infectious ME/CFS and in post-COVID patients with post-exertional malaise. The **dopamine pathway** (dopamine plus its metabolites DOPAC and HVA) was statistically indistinguishable from healthy controls (@Aregawi2026Noradrenergic). Within the post-COVID group, only the subgroup with PEM was low.

**Why selectivity matters.** Norepinephrine is made *from* dopamine by an enzyme called dopamine-β-hydroxylase (DBH). DBH sits *inside* synaptic vesicles. But dopamine must first be pumped into the vesicle by a different protein, **VMAT2**, powered by an ATP-driven proton gradient; cytoplasmic dopamine never needs that transport step.

A shortage of **energy at the vesicle** would therefore impair the dopamine-to-norepinephrine conversion while leaving dopamine itself intact. That is *one* plausible mechanism — others include reduced DBH, altered reuptake, or cofactor loss — for the selective pattern observed. It is consistent with a disease built on an energy-supply problem; it is not proven.

**The caveats.** The study was small (n=16 in the ME/CFS arm), from a single centre, used a novel composite index, and has not been independently replicated. Physical deconditioning could lower norepinephrine without causing symptoms; that confound has not been eliminated. The *selectivity* is the most interesting part of the finding — and the part most in need of replication.
